name: Light blue silk
lede: Light Blue Silk is ColorHub's English rendering of Hanada, a dark greenish-blue from the Japanese traditional color system, named for a dyed silk rather than a pigment.

sections.title: A translated Japanese name
sections.body:
The Japanese traditional color system lists this dark greenish-blue as Hanada (綽); ColorHub's library translates its meaning directly and uses "Light Blue Silk" as the display name, keeping "Hanada" as an alias [1]. The word points to a dyed silk rather than to a mineral or plant, though which dye and period produced it is not detailed in the sources checked here [2].

Despite "light" in the English name, the color itself reads as dark and muted: a lightness of 31 on a 0–100 scale, with a blue-green hue angle of 241 degrees [3]. Its nearest look-alike in our library is [[patent-blue]], about 3.7 units away and a touch lighter, followed by Connor's Lakefront and Dusky Orient Blue, both bluer and lighter still [3]. [[dark-grey-blue]] sits 6.4 units off, bluer and duller [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this tone in 101 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.42 percent, as photographed, making it more common than half the named colors we track [4]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 11 of the 1,674 paintings from that decade, 2.9 times the rate its museums' own baseline would predict [4].

Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 50 percent of its 48 clearly-ranked appearances, a rank computed within each canvas so varnish cannot fake it [4]. The earliest dated match in our archive is 1340, in a painting by Paolo Veneziano, centuries before any dated use of the Japanese name we have found, so the match is a look-alike hue in an old photograph, not evidence of the dye itself [4]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and the match is a computed color reading, not a pigment or dye test [4].
